system:
You write serialized fiction for audio-first mobile readers: 400-700 word episodes, read in
two or three minutes, each one ending on a hook strong enough to make someone tap "next".

Craft rules that matter more than anything else:
- Concrete over abstract. Specific objects, sounds, names, times, prices, street details. No generic mood fog.
- Every scene turns: someone wants something, something blocks it, the situation is different at the end.
- Subtext in dialogue. People dodge, lie, interrupt. Nobody explains the plot to someone who already knows it.
- Earn the hook from inside the episode. The final beat changes what the reader believes or fears.
- Momentum: enter scenes late, leave early. No recaps of the previous episode beyond one anchoring line.
- Never contradict established canon. If canon is silent, you may invent — but keep it small and consistent.

You are the showrunner. Given a one-line premise, design a series bible that can sustain
200 episodes without running out of story: a central mystery with a satisfying hidden truth,
6-10 core characters with conflicting wants and real secrets, 3-6 recurring locations, world
rules that constrain the supernatural or central conceit, and 10-16 story threads (mystery,
relationship, antagonist, personal) with planned introduction and payoff episodes spread across
episodes 1-200. Thread codes are T01, T02, ... Include 10-20 banned clichés specific to this genre.

The engine of a long serial is people, not paperwork: drive the mystery through desire, jealousy, love,
greed, family loyalty, shame and betrayal between characters the audience cares about. Institutions, records
and procedures may appear as obstacles, never as the heart of the story. If a creative brief is given, its
setting, culture, names and tone are binding.
user:
Premise: In a sleepy hill town, a newlywed who devours cheap crime novels becomes the prime suspect when her husband's charred body is found — but the next morning, her phone rings with his voice.

Creative brief (binding): Bollywood pulp-noir romantic thriller in the spirit of Haseen Dillruba, original story. Fictional Himachal hill town, Indian joint family, passionate suspicious marriage, jealous ex-lover, twisty family secrets, dark humour, occasional Hindi words.

Total episodes: 200. Design the series bible.

{
  "title": "The Husband Who Called at Dawn",
  "logline": "In a Himachal hill town, newlywed Meher Sood is accused of burning her husband alive. At 6:12 the next morning, he calls her. His return clears up one lie and traps their joint family inside a far older one.",
  "genre": "Bollywood pulp-noir romantic thriller",
  "tone": "Sensuous, sharp, suspicious and darkly funny; domestic tenderness can turn dangerous between one line of dialogue and the next.",
  "pov_and_tense": "Close third person, past tense, principally Meher's. Occasional Tara, Aadit and Kavya episodes reveal their choices without disclosing the killer early.",
  "setting": "Kesarghat, a fictional Himachal apple town above a winding bus road. Its Lower Bazaar sells rain covers, stove wicks and ₹40 crime paperbacks. At Cedar Terrace, four generations' worth of belongings crowd a house occupied by one family that cannot agree who belongs in it.",
  "world_rules": [
    "There is no supernatural element. Aadit's dawn call is live, made from a bus driver's borrowed phone; the number is traceable.",
    "Fire damages evidence but does not abolish forensics. The body's identification as Aadit is provisional, based on his coat and wedding ring, and is challenged early.",
    "A road closure can delay someone for hours, not make them disappear for months. Secrets persist because people protect relationships, not because phones or investigators stop working.",
    "Parentage can be tested. The obstacle is getting the adults responsible for Keshav to consent and live with the answer, not locating a magical document.",
    "An eight-year-old can notice a quarrel or hide a keepsake; Keshav is never made responsible for solving a murder or choosing which mother deserves him."
  ],
  "truth": "Eight years before the fire, Shanta took the living newborn son of Aadit and his then-lover Tara. She told each parent the baby had died and gave him to her grieving elder son Raghav and daughter-in-law Kavya as a supposedly surrendered infant. They raised him as Keshav. Kavya learned his parentage two years before the series begins but kept silent: he was her son in every daily sense she understood. Tara's brother Manu discovered the deception shortly before Meher's wedding. He took money to postpone telling Tara, then changed his mind. On the night of the fire, Aadit confronted Manu at the apple-drying shed and left knowing only that his child might be alive. Kavya met Manu afterward. When he said Tara would learn the truth the next morning, Kavya struck him fatally with an iron crate hook. She burned the body in Aadit's coat and ring, both taken from the Sood house, and planted a piece of Meher's shawl. She meant to direct suspicion away from herself long enough to move Keshav, not to sustain a false identification forever. Aadit, frightened by what Manu had told him and by the fire, hid overnight and called Meher before returning. Meher discovers that her husband was alive, then who died, then why: three answers that cost the family more than the initial accusation. Kavya ultimately admits the killing; Shanta admits the abduction. Neither confession erases Kavya's years of mothering or Tara's loss. By episode 200, Keshav knows his history, the responsible adults face consequences, and Meher and Aadit choose a marriage without protective lies.",
  "characters": [
    {
      "name": "Meher Sood, née Bedi, 29",
      "role": "Newlywed, paperback obsessive and initial murder suspect",
      "description": "Keeps a pencil in the spine of whatever lurid novel she is reading. Came to Kesarghat expecting a difficult marriage, not a corpse wearing her husband's ring.",
      "want": "Clear her name and find out whether Aadit married her while still in love with Tara.",
      "need": "Stop treating people as plots she can solve without asking them what they want.",
      "secret": "She anonymously writes crime-paperback chapters for extra money; one published scene describes a wife faking her husband's death in a fire.",
      "series_arc": "From a bride defending herself in someone else's house to a partner who can leave, stay or tell her own story by choice.",
      "voice": "Quick, observant, dry under pressure. Her jokes arrive a second before her fear does."
    },
    {
      "name": "Aadit Sood, 33",
      "role": "Meher's husband; apparent victim and actual dawn caller",
      "description": "Runs the family's apple business with his elder brother. He is generous in public and evasive at the kitchen table.",
      "want": "Keep Meher, find the child Manu hinted was alive, and avoid destroying the family that raised him.",
      "need": "Tell the truth before deciding whom it might hurt.",
      "secret": "He met Manu at the shed before the killing. He stayed hidden overnight after the fire and let Meher face suspicion rather than explain Tara and the child.",
      "series_arc": "Returns alive by episode 8, but has to earn back the much harder belief that he will stay and speak plainly.",
      "voice": "Warm and persuasive until cornered; then abruptly precise."
    },
    {
      "name": "Tara Thakur, 32",
      "role": "Aadit's former lover; Manu's sister",
      "description": "Runs Anardana Dhaba at the bus bend. She can tell a driver by the sound of his horn and still cannot bear the smell of hospital soap.",
      "want": "Find Manu's killer and recover what was taken from her without begging the Soods for either answer.",
      "need": "Make room for Keshav's existing attachments, including one she has reason to hate.",
      "secret": "She kept one unsent letter asking Aadit to run away with her after the birth she believed ended in death.",
      "series_arc": "Neither a romantic obstacle nor a saint: she gains a son, loses the fantasy of getting his first eight years back, and builds a relationship on the years ahead.",
      "voice": "Blunt, funny, sparing with names; she uses 'ji' when she means the opposite."
    },
    {
      "name": "Shanta Sood, 61",
      "role": "Matriarch of Cedar Terrace",
      "description": "Counts household sugar by the tin and remembers every guest's preferred pickle. Her acts of care are real; so is her capacity to control.",
      "want": "Keep her sons, their marriages and Keshav under one roof.",
      "need": "Admit that saving a family cannot mean stealing a child and calling it love.",
      "secret": "She took Tara's newborn and told both birth parents he had died.",
      "series_arc": "Loses the power to define the family by herself and eventually tells the truth without bargaining for forgiveness.",
      "voice": "Soft instructions that sound like blessings until someone disobeys."
    },
    {
      "name": "Raghav Sood, 39",
      "role": "Aadit's elder brother and Keshav's father",
      "description": "Handles the sorting shed, the creditors and Keshav's school shoes. He believes endurance entitles him to trust.",
      "want": "Keep the orchard solvent and his wife and son safe.",
      "need": "Understand that loyalty becomes cowardice when it requires someone else to bear the harm.",
      "secret": "He saw Kavya near the shed that night and gave her an alibi, believing he was concealing an affair. He thinks Keshav's birth parents willingly surrendered him.",
      "series_arc": "His alibi breaks his marriage open; his decision to consent to Keshav's parentage test makes a different kind of fatherhood possible.",
      "voice": "Short figures and practical questions in place of apologies."
    },
    {
      "name": "Kavya Sood, 36",
      "role": "Raghav's wife, Keshav's mother and the killer",
      "description": "Mends school uniforms so neatly the repair becomes the strongest seam. She has raised Keshav since infancy.",
      "want": "Keep the child she loves from being taken out of her home.",
      "need": "Recognize that Keshav can love her without being kept ignorant or captive.",
      "secret": "She learned who his birth parents were two years ago. She killed Manu when he insisted on telling Tara, then staged the fire.",
      "series_arc": "A formidable parent whose possessiveness leads to murder. Her confession is a choice to stop making Keshav carry her lies, not a bid for instant absolution.",
      "voice": "Measured and hospitable; the sharper her fear, the more politely she offers tea."
    },
    {
      "name": "Keshav 'Kesu' Sood, 8",
      "role": "Raghav and Kavya's son; Tara and Aadit's biological child",
      "description": "Collects bus tickets and carves crooked birds from fallen walnut twigs. Knows which floorboard creaks outside his bedroom.",
      "want": "Have his school picnic attended without the adults quarrelling.",
      "need": "Be given an honest account of his life at a pace he can bear.",
      "secret": "He sometimes visits Tara's dhaba for sweet lime without telling Kavya, because she becomes quiet afterward.",
      "series_arc": "Remains a child with games, loyalties and ordinary demands while the adults learn that knowing his origins does not require him to stop loving anyone.",
      "voice": "Literal, curious and resistant to questions with an obvious preferred answer."
    },
    {
      "name": "Naina Sood, 25",
      "role": "Youngest Sood sibling",
      "description": "Repairs customers' phones at a Lower Bazaar counter and is treated at home as though she still breaks them.",
      "want": "Be trusted as an adult without having to abandon Cedar Terrace.",
      "need": "Let Manu be remembered truthfully rather than as either her great love or the family's convenient villain.",
      "secret": "She had a brief relationship with Manu and arranged his meeting with Kavya on the night he died.",
      "series_arc": "Her silence initially protects her reputation; telling the family what Manu intended helps strip their excuses away.",
      "voice": "Fast interruptions, technical comparisons, sudden uncomfortable honesty."
    },
    {
      "name": "Bhuvan Negi, 52",
      "role": "Kesarghat police inspector; Tara and Manu's maternal uncle",
      "description": "Keeps peppermints in his uniform pocket and knows which local witnesses will refuse a second cup of tea.",
      "want": "Find Manu's killer without letting his own earlier failure decide the case.",
      "need": "Be an uncle who tells Tara an ugly truth, not an officer who quietly manages it for her.",
      "secret": "Years earlier, he gave Manu money to leave town after a theft and lied to Tara that her brother had gone of his own accord.",
      "series_arc": "Starts the fire investigation, steps aside when Manu is identified, and remains a fallible member of the family the case has wounded.",
      "voice": "Patient questions, bone-dry observations; never a grand speech about justice."
    }
  ],
  "locations": [
    {
      "name": "Cedar Terrace",
      "description": "The Soods' crowded slate-roof house: pickle jars along the veranda, shoes beneath the dining bench, and too few doors for anyone to keep a quarrel private."
    },
    {
      "name": "Bagh Number Seven",
      "description": "The apple orchard and old wood-fired drying shed where the body burns. By harvest, the family must decide whether they can work the same trees together."
    },
    {
      "name": "Anardana Dhaba",
      "description": "Tara's six-table stop at Do-Mile Bend, with a tin roof, impatient bus drivers and a view of the road into town."
    },
    {
      "name": "Lower Bazaar",
      "description": "A steep row of phone-repair counters, paperback racks, vegetable crates and shutters that turn every whispered accusation into public entertainment."
    },
    {
      "name": "The Walnut Steps",
      "description": "Seventy-three worn steps between Cedar Terrace and the bus road. Children use them as a shortcut; adults use them when they do not want to arrive together."
    }
  ],
  "threads": [
    {

      "title": "The body in Aadit's ring",

      "payoff_ep": 99
    },

      "title": "Meher's other name",

      "title": "The price of the orchard",

      "code": "T13",
      "title": "Raghav's alibi",

      "code": "T14",
      "title": "Who killed Manu?",
      "description": "Suspicion passes through the people Manu loved, threatened and disappointed. Confronted with the cost of another lie to Keshav, Kavya admits the fatal blow and the fire.",

      "payoff_ep": 188

    {
      "code": "T15",
      "title": "Kavya after the confession",
      "description": "Her account is checked against the hidden broken hook. Raghav and Tara reject both revenge through Keshav and the pretense that his mother did nothing wrong.",
      "introduce_by_ep": 13,
      "payoff_ep": 193

    {
      "code": "T16",
      "title": "A marriage without alibis",
      "description": "Meher and Aadit repeatedly choose honesty when silence would be easier. They end the series together on terms Meher can name, within a family Keshav is allowed to define for himself.",
      "introduce_by_ep": 1,
      "payoff_ep": 200
    }
  ],
  "style_guide": [
    "Episodes run 400–700 words, usually one or two scenes. Enter after the polite conversation has failed; leave when a choice or discovery changes its cost.",
    "Put desire in the room: someone wants the ring back, a seat at a picnic, ₹8,000 by Friday, or one answer before the tea goes cold.",
    "Build hooks from a changed relationship or a newly dangerous fact, not a random knock at the door.",
    "Let Meher's paperback knowledge help her notice practical details, then mislead her when she assumes people behave like characters.",
    "Use Hindi naturally and sparingly—arre, bas, achha, ji—without pausing to translate what context makes clear.",
    "Keep the comedy specific: disputed pressure-cooker whistles, a bus driver offended by being called a witness, Shanta correcting someone's pickle recipe during an accusation.",
    "Give Manu a lived past through Tara, Naina and Bhuvan. He was neither a disposable corpse nor secretly innocent of every harm.",
    "Track who knows each family secret. A character may lie about a fact they know, but cannot reveal one they have not learned."
  ],
  "banned_phrases": [
    "It was all a dream.",
    "The husband has a secret identical twin.",
    "His voice was an AI imitation.",
    "A ghost made the dawn call.",
    "The heroine conveniently loses her memory of the fire.",
    "A surprise serial killer explains every unrelated act.",
    "One perfect dying recording explains the whole plot.",
    "A birthmark substitutes for proof of parentage.",
    "Forensics are unavailable for 180 episodes without a reason.",
    "An evil saas acts only because she hates her daughter-in-law.",
    "Infertility or pregnancy loss is treated as a cause of wickedness.",
    "The jealous ex exists only to steal the husband.",
    "Aadit rescues Meher from a mystery she was solving herself.",
    "Keshav is made to choose his 'real' mother on command.",
    "A confession at gunpoint replaces earned discovery.",
    "Every road is blocked whenever a plot needs someone stranded.",
    "A conveniently discovered will settles an emotional conflict.",
    "Love excuses kidnapping or murder."
  ],
  "motifs": [
    "A gold ring that survives a fire but cannot identify its wearer",
    "Walnut birds carved with imperfect wings",
    "Bus tickets kept long after a journey ends",
    "Coats borrowed without asking",
    "Paperbacks with spectacular covers and surprisingly useful observations",
    "A pressure cooker whose whistle interrupts the worst possible sentence"
  ]
